column6: The commentary joins a received text, reverent fear, and active response; the king reads the written Torah daily precisely to learn fear of YHWH and keep its words.
The commentary's unnamed listener is defined by an inward reverence rather than a social label; Isaiah likewise singles out the humble and contrite person who trembles at YHWH's word.
Like the commentary's limit on the messenger's task, Ezekiel has warned the wicked; if the hearer does not turn, he dies for his own wrong while the watchman is delivered.

column5: hear words but heart pursues gain
column6: The people sit before Ezekiel and hear his words but do not do them because their hearts pursue gain, a direct scene of speech reaching listeners without becoming received instruction.

The announced word did not benefit its hearers because it was not joined with faith, closely matching the commentary's distinction between an offered reminder and one that benefits a receptive person.
Jesus's good soil hears the word, holds it fast in an honest and good heart, and bears fruit in perseverance; this gives the commentary's inward taking-up of admonition a concrete narrative figure.
James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the doer who perseveres, directly joining the commentary's memory-versus-forgetting image to the listener's own enacted response.
The blessing falls on reader, hearers, and keepers together, a close Christian chain from spoken written warning through reception to practice.

column5: tender heart when book is heard
column6: Josiah's tender, humbled heart responds when he hears the words of judgment from the book, supplying a biblical portrait of the inward disposition through which admonition takes effect.
The psalm's urgent today makes hearing a timely act, closely paralleling the commentary's near-future remembrance before the moment for response has passed.
The command not to harden the heart names the inward contrary to the commentary's reverent listener who can receive a reminder.
The Torah requires its words to be upon the heart, a precise counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the listener must carry the reminder within rather than merely hear it pass by.
After the words are placed on the heart, they are repeated and spoken through daily life; this illuminates the commentary's path from inward remembrance back to voiced practice.
Joshua is told to keep the book on his mouth, meditate on it continually, and do it, a compact analogue for the commentary's movement from transmitted speech through inner recollection to action.
The psalmist stores YHWH's word in the heart in order not to sin, giving the commentary's retained rather than lost reminder a moral consequence.
The explicit resolve not to forget the divine word directly accompanies the commentary's ذ ك ر B003 contrast between holding what one has received and letting it escape.

column5: ذ ك ر B003 and Hebrew זכר
column6: The source label ذ ك ر B003 concerns remembering and holding; the Hebrew cognate זכר commands active Sabbath remembrance that takes ritual form in sanctifying the day.
Those who fear YHWH speak with one another, and a book of remembrance is written before him; the Hebrew זכר family brings together fear, voiced attention, and memorial record.

column5: remember what was received and heard
column6: The church is told to remember how it received and heard, then keep it and repent, directly framing remembrance as recovery of a previously received word that still demands action.
The command to remember the height from which one has fallen and return to first works closely matches the commentary's tezekkür as seeking and recovering what has slipped away.

The person lacking virtue is blind and has forgotten cleansing from former sins, an unusually close counterpart to the commentary's pairing of remembered truth with opened sight and later purification.
Jesus joins unseeing eyes, unhearing ears, and failure to remember in one rebuke, closely matching the commentary's contrast between a reminder that opens sight and refusal that does not truly hear.
Isaiah's hardened heart, heavy ears, and shut eyes prevent hearing, seeing, understanding, and turning; it is the negative counterpart to the commentary's inward alertness becoming sight.
Hebrews requires closer attention to what was heard lest it drift away, giving a specific image for the commentary's concern that a received thing can escape unless the listener holds it.
After Jesus's resurrection the disciples remember his saying and believe Scripture and his word, a narrative in which recall of a prior utterance becomes renewed understanding and trust.
Job identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding, directly supporting the commentary's claim that reverent fear is bound to knowledge rather than mere fright.
The psalm makes fear of YHWH the beginning of wisdom, a concise biblical formulation for the commentary's knowledgeable, reality-responsive fear.

YHWH promises to place his fear in the people's hearts so that they will not turn away, paralleling the commentary's presentation of fear as an enduring inward condition that yields faithful response.
YHWH's intimate counsel and covenant are made known to those who fear him, linking fear with the knowing and receiving of divine instruction developed in the commentary.
Moses distinguishes immediate panic from fear of God set before Israel so that they do not sin, clarifying the commentary's distinction between ordinary fright and reverent, morally active fear.

column5: warning about unseen things and reverence
column6: Noah is warned about things not yet seen and, acting in reverent fear, prepares the ark; this is a close figure for remembering and fearing before judgment becomes visible.

column5: gentle correction toward repentance and knowledge
column6: Gentle instruction is offered in hope that God may grant repentance leading to knowledge of truth, closely echoing the commentary's soft speech to Pharaoh as a possible door into recollection or fear.

column5: coming to one's senses from the devil's snare
column6: The corrected opponents may come to their senses and escape the devil's snare, a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's temptation-triggered remembering, renewed sight, and recovery.

column5: Moses and Aaron before hardened Pharaoh
column6: Against the commentary's Qur'anic scene of gentle speech offered in hope that Pharaoh may remember or fear, Exodus's shared mission reports Pharaoh's hardened heart and refusal to listen; the differing outcome is the point of the comparison.
Habakkuk hears YHWH's report and responds with awe, supplying the inverse sequence explicitly considered in the commentary: revelation remembered or heard can awaken fear.
Personified Wisdom calls and stretches out a hand but is refused, a pointed counterpart to the commentary's reminder that can be offered by a speaker yet passed by by its audience.
After calamity those who rejected Wisdom call and seek, but receive no answer; it closely parallels the commentary's warning that remembrance after the decisive moment no longer benefits.
The refusal of Wisdom is explained as hatred of knowledge and refusal to choose fear of YHWH, tightly combining the commentary's two central inward conditions.

column5: refused call and unanswered later call
column6: Because the people did not hear when YHWH called, he would not hear when they later called, giving the commentary's timely-warning and too-late-response structure a prophetic counterpart.

column5: remember the Creator before evil days
column6: Qohelet commands remembrance of the Creator while life still affords response, directly matching the commentary's contrast between present remembrance and regret after the time has passed.
Esau seeks the blessing afterward but finds no place for repentance despite tears, a specific New Testament image for the commentary's ineffectual late turning.
Israel's claim that its own power produced wealth gives the commentary's self-sufficient figure a close Torah counterpart: perceived sufficiency obscures dependence and remembrance.
The command to remember YHWH as giver of power directly answers the self-credit of the preceding verse, like the commentary's call to recover what self-sufficiency refuses to see.

Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing, while not knowing it is poor and blind; this is an exceptionally close counterpart to the commentary's self-satisfied person who sees no lack and so does not seek what was lost.

column5: eye salve so that you may see
column6: The counsel to anoint blind eyes so that they may see continues the Laodicean contrast and concretizes the commentary's image of recollection opening the eye.

column5: remembering the Name and keeping Torah
column6: The psalmist remembers YHWH's name in the night and keeps Torah, a direct analogue for the commentary's final movement from inward recollection to voiced divine name and obedient practice.

column5: praise joined to not forgetting benefits
column6: The soul blesses YHWH by not forgetting his benefits, making praise itself an answer to retained memory as in the commentary's zikir moving back into speech.

The word dwelling richly in the community produces teaching, admonition, and sung gratitude, closely paralleling the commentary's arc from spoken reminder through inward retention to worshipful speech.
The command to perform the meal in remembrance of Christ gives the commentary's move from recall to a repeated act of worship a specific Christian liturgical form.
The Messiah sanctifies and cleanses through the word, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's sequence in which a received reminder leads on toward purification.
The individual who sins bears his own iniquity, directly illuminating the commentary's insistence that the unresponsive hearer, rather than the warning messenger, carries the consequence.
Paul's maxim that each person carries his own load supplies a New Testament ethical analogue for the commentary's refusal to shift the listener's response or burden onto another.

The grass withers while God's word stands forever, a close counterpart to the surah's meadow turning to refuse and the commentary's contrast between perishing natural forms and a retained divine word.

column5: active salvation with fear and trembling
column6: Believers are told to work out salvation with fear and trembling, bringing together the commentary's inward reverence and the listener's personal, active response.
Receiving the unshakable kingdom issues in acceptable worship with reverence and awe, closely corresponding to the commentary's movement from fear and remembrance into prayerful praise.

column5: fear God, give glory, judgment near
column6: The angelic proclamation calls people to fear God and give him glory because judgment has come, an explicit fusion of warning, reverent response, and imminent eschatological time.
The psalmist's flesh trembles from fear of YHWH and his judgments, giving the commentary's bodily shudder of reverent hearers a direct biblical analogue.
Habakkuk's body and lips tremble when he hears, a concrete parallel to the commentary's account of hearing that first causes bodily trembling before a later inward response.

column5: Spirit teaching and bringing words to memory
column6: Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach the disciples and bring his sayings to their remembrance; this places divine agency alongside the commentary's distinction between transmitted speech and the hearer's remembering.
The women remember Jesus's earlier words at the empty tomb, a narrative recovery of a prior utterance that changes how they understand the present event.
In the temptation scene Jesus answers Satan by voicing Scripture and commanding worship of God alone, a specific image of retained divine words resisting a satanic prompt.

Abraham tells the rich man to remember his former life after he is in torment, making explicit the commentary's contrast between useful present recollection and a painful, irreversible memory after judgment.

column5: refusal to hear Moses and the prophets
column6: The claim that one who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection speaks to the commentary's image of people passing by an offered reminder while desiring a more exceptional sign.

column5: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: YHWH's song is promised not to be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a Torah image for preserving a divinely given utterance across forgetting and recitation.
The fading grass image recalls the commentary's meadow becoming refuse; Peter uses it to frame the transience of human life before the enduring proclaimed word in the following verse.

column5: abiding word proclaimed as good news
column6: The word of the Lord remains forever and is identified as the good news preached to the hearers, a Christian counterpart to the enduring, transmitted reminder set against perishing grass.
The text argues that the greatness and beauty of creatures lead to perception of their Maker, closely serving the commentary's claim that attentive knowledge of creation can ground reverent fear.
Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa says that wisdom endures when fear of sin precedes it, a later Jewish ethical formulation that sharpens the commentary's ordering of inward fear before receptive understanding.
The mishnah extends remembrance of the exodus into nighttime recitation, a Jewish liturgical interpretation that helps illuminate the commentary's passage from memory into spoken devotion.

column5: fear of Heaven and human responsibility
column6: The rabbinic maxim that all is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven gives a pointed later formulation for the commentary's tension between the listener's responsibility and divine sovereignty.

Augustine describes finding God in memory after learning him, a Christian theological reflection that enriches the commentary's claim that remembrance is an active return toward what one has received and lost.

column5: heart to know, eyes to see, ears to hear
column6: Moses says that Israel has not been given a heart to know, eyes to see, or ears to hear; this complicates and deepens the commentary's discussion of listenerly response as occurring within divine willing.

column5: lips near, heart distant, learned fear
column6: Isaiah contrasts lip service and a distant heart with a fear learned as human command, a counter-image to the commentary's knowledge-born, inwardly real reverence.
Because forgiveness is with YHWH, he is feared; this supplies another of the commentary's possible sequences, where awareness of God's act awakens reverence rather than merely following it.

column5: rejected word judging on the last day
column6: Jesus says the word he has spoken will judge the one who rejects it on the last day, linking the commentary's non-coercive warning to its theme of a final moment when response is no longer open.
